We are high school students from New Jersey. 

James is a high school junior interested in AI, robotics, and CS. He has competed at the VEX Robotics World Championships three times and won several international awards. He develops full-stack apps, websites, and hardware for fun. 

Victor is a high school sophomore interested in AI and CS. He is especially interested in the math behind AI and loves building anything from ML models to full stack websites!
summary:
Artemis crews and Mars rover teams train on Earth first. Common Ground helps them find the places on Earth whose terrain best matches the Moon and Mars. The user can click any spot on our 3D globe, and the app lifts out a 4 km block of terrain from around it. It compares that block with 4,636 blocks from NASA LRO, JAXA Kaguya, MRO, and Mars Global Surveyor terrain. It measures slope, roughness, landform shape, and shadow under a Sun 1.5 to 5 degrees above the horizon, the lighting at the lunar south pole.

Our model splits each block into 64 cells and pairs them with the cells of every Moon and Mars block. It then scores 8 regions and 34 landforms. The score is a sum, with the bars on screen adding up to the exact score.

On areas the model never saw in training, verified analog sites ranked in the top 3% of Earth land. A global search found 175 candidates in 38 countries on no analog list we used, such as a lunar south pole match at 21.56° S, 68.34° W in northern Chile. Every candidate is ranked on our Best Sites page.
details:
We wanted to build a tool to tell Artemis crews and Mars rover teams where on Earth they should train before they fly, down to one crater or one ridge.

Artemis crews and Mars rover teams train on Earth before they fly. We wanted to build a tool to find places beyond the well-studied sites like Atacama and Iceland, and tell them where on Earth they should train before they fly, down to one crater or one ridge.  

Common Ground opens on a 3D globe of Earth, the Moon and Mars, built on CesiumJS. From far out, Earth shows NASA's Blue Marble from GIBS. Click a spot on land and the camera flies down. The 4 km block around your click lifts out of the planet as a unique floating diorama with walls, so you see its relief from the side. 

The result panel has tabs for both Moon and Mars, each with four regions. The Moon regions are lunar maria, lunar highlands, impact basin rings and ejecta, and the south polar region. The Mars regions are the southern cratered highlands, northern lowlands, volcanic provinces, and outflow channels and chaos. Each region gets an overall similarity score for the Earth location you picked, built from a terrain score and a surface score. Below the scores, the app lists the closest real lunar or Martian places by their IAU Gazetteer names, for example, "crater rim, 12 km from Tycho". A second score rates one landform inside the region, such as a crater rim, wrinkle ridge, graben, sinuous rille, or yardang.

We split each 4 km block into 64 500 m cells and assign each cell 9 terrain features. These include slope, roughness, convex and concave curvature, relative height at two distances, height within the block, and shadow under two Suns: one at mid-height and one 1.5 to 5 degrees above the horizon. We use 15 more numbers to describe the whole block: relief, Hurst exponent, linearity, the area and depth of closed depressions, how bowl- and cone-shaped it is, and how its relief splits across scales. The same code computes all of this on Earth, Moon, and Mars terrain. We also score a wider 32 km block at 250 m, so the app sees the region around your click.

To compare two blocks, we pair their 64 cells with exact optimal matching (the Hungarian method, which gives a 2-Wasserstein distance). This lets a hummocky crater floor match another hummocky floor even when the bumps are in different positions. A 32-number sketch picks 100 candidates first, reducing the response time by removing the need to check all 4,636 potential options. 

In the matching model, every input passes through a curve that can only go one way. More mismatch can only lower the match. Each region score then adds that match to a terrain model trained on real analog sites, so every part of the score is a sum. The overall score is the region score to the power 0.8 times the surface score to the power 0.2, so a forest can drag a good landscape down, but bare ground can't save a bad one.

Because the score is a sum, the app can explain it exactly. The bars start from ordinary land and add one bar per measurement. They end on the exact number shown, because the bars are the model. We’re most proud of our visualization. Common Ground automatically renders the closest Moon or Mars block as a wireframe over your selected Earth block, rotated to fit, letting you see how well the shapes fit with each other. The block includes numbered points that show the points that helped or hurt the match, letting the user take note of how much each terrain inconsistency affected the score.

Since we're students doing research ourselves, we made every result exportable. The user can download a CSV, the full JSON, or a one-page printable field sheet for a class or a field team, allowing them to use data from our models in other academic research.

Our site includes two more pages. “Best Sites” lists the top Earth blocks for each region and each validated landform, from a search of all land on Earth. Picks sit at least 50 km apart, with no more than 4 per country. “How We Know” shows all of our validation numbers. All of our code, including the training notebook, is public on the GitHub repository linked on the site.

We trained the terrain model on verified analog sites against random land, with volcanoes from the Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program and known impact craters as weaker examples. A separate surface model reads ESA WorldCover land cover and WorldClim rainfall. The labels come from planetary science. Moon and Mars regions come from the USGS geologic maps of the Moon (2020) and Mars (Tanaka et al. 2014). Landform tags come from the Robbins crater databases (1.3 million lunar and 385,000 Martian craters), mapped ridges, grabens and rilles, and the IAU Gazetteer. The library holds 2,236 Moon blocks and 2,400 Mars blocks from JAXA Kaguya terrain models, LRO LOLA, MRO CTX, and MGS MOLA blended with Mars Express HRSC. We filtered every DEM to the same effective resolution, so the models compare terrain.

We test by area. All sites and land inside the same 6 degree cell are held out together, across 5 folds and 3 splits, so every number here comes from a model that never saw that part of the world. Our current model puts verified analog sites at a median of the top 2.9% of Earth land, with 73% in the top 10%. Verified sites get a median overall score of 69, and random land gets 26. Before scoring our nine check sites, we wrote down the order we expected, and the model matches it with a Spearman correlation of 0.78. Dutch farmland scores 5, the Amazon 6, Timanfaya 78, and the McMurdo Dry Valleys 81. On 21 sites from an expert list we never trained on, Mauna Kea scores 94, Atacama Yungay 79, and Askja 77. 19 of our 34 landforms pass validation.

The challenge says rediscovering famous sites isn't the goal, so we searched all land on Earth. For lunar maria alone, our global search ranked 3,697 candidates. In total, our app found 175 candidates in 38 countries that appear on no analog list we used. A few of the strongest show the range. A block at 21.56° S, 68.34° W, on the high plateau northeast of Calama, Chile, matches the lunar south polar region: its steep walls and deep closed hollows fill with long shadows under a Sun a few degrees above the horizon. A block at 25.93° S, 68.87° W, northeast of Diego de Almagro, Chile, is a top match for the lunar highlands. Blocks at 26.82° S, 68.52° W in Argentina and 36.80° N, 117.75° W in eastern California match impact basin rings and ejecta, with rough, rubbly ground full of closed hollows and almost no plants. The full rankings for every region and landform are on our Best Sites page, and each entry opens its own result page with the bars that explain its score.

With Common Ground, mission planners and scientists can find Earth's best analog sites, see each one beside its Moon or Mars match through the wireframe overlay, and understand which measurements make a spot more or less useful for training. Field teams can also check a site before they travel. 

Most similarity tools we looked at give you one number. Common Ground shows and explains the model's own math. Cell pairing by optimal transport compares the mix of ground in two blocks, wherever each bump sits. We measure shadow under a Sun 1.5 to 5 degrees up, which is how the lunar south pole is lit. We haven't seen another team do that. The lifted diorama, the wireframe, and Moon light are all unique and let you see the comparison in 3D instead of reading a number.

The front end uses TypeScript, Next.js, React, and Tailwind. The globes run on CesiumJS with Cesium World Terrain, Moon, and Mars. The blocks use three.js with react-three-fiber, and the charts use Recharts. The site is hosted on Vercel. The back end is Python with FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, and pyproj, in Docker on Render. Our model’s scores are all cached on Supabase, and Cloudflare R2 holds the model file and height grids.

The ML pipeline is one Jupyter notebook, public in the repository linked on the site. It builds the library, trains both models, runs every check, and writes the validation file. The server runs the same scoring file the notebook trains with, so training and serving can't drift apart. We built everything on our laptops with no paid GPU.

We also planned for real use. Each click reads Copernicus GLO-30 and ESA WorldCover from public AWS buckets. WorldCover stops at 60 degrees south, so our first model read the Dry Valleys as solid snow. We fixed that by treating Antarctic blocks as free of trees, crops, and buildings.
